Reading Is Different
for Everyone Understanding Dyslexia

Reading is often treated as a simple everyday activity. We read messages, signs, articles, instructions and social media posts without thinking much about the process behind it. However, reading does not feel the same for everyone.

"Literacy is multi-dimensional. How our eyes and minds process written symbols varies naturally across every individual."

Executive Summary Key Takeaways
  • Definition: Dyslexia is a natural neurodivergent processing difference, not a reflection of intelligence or effort (International Dyslexia Association, 2026).
  • Prevalence: It affects approximately 10% of people (around 1 in 10 in classrooms and workplaces) (British Dyslexia Association, 2026).
  • Accessibility: Line guides, audio support, extra processing time, and clean layouts make learning accessible to all (W3C, 2026).

Some people can move through a paragraph quickly and smoothly. Others may pause at individual words, reread the same sentence or need more time to process what they have read. This does not mean that they are careless, unintelligent or unwilling to learn. For some readers, these experiences may be connected to dyslexia.

1 What Is Dyslexia?

Dyslexia is a learning difference that mainly affects reading, spelling and writing (International Dyslexia Association, 2026). It may cause difficulties with recognising words accurately, reading fluently, sounding out unfamiliar words and processing written language (World Health Organization, 2026). Dyslexia may also affect how a person remembers and organises information.

Neurodiversity Insight Visualizing Word Processing
Visual Word Form Pathway

Automatic recognition linking letters straight to word concepts and sound patterns rapidly.

Multi-Step Decoding Pathway

Additional steps required to break down phonemes, sound out syllables, and sequence written symbols.

A person with dyslexia may understand an idea clearly but require more time to read or communicate it in writing. Dyslexia is not caused by laziness, carelessness or a lack of effort. It also does not determine a person’s intelligence or potential for success (Eide & Eide, 2026).

Dyslexia affects individuals differently. Some people experience mild difficulties, while others may require more consistent support when reading, studying or completing written tasks.

2 How Reading May Feel

Consider this simple sentence:

Fluent Reading Pattern

"The cat sat on the mat."

A fluent reader may recognise the words immediately and read the whole sentence smoothly.

Dyslexic Processing Experience
The… cat… sat… on… the mat.

The reader may pause, check a word, lose their place, reread part of the sentence and then continue. They may eventually understand exactly the same message, but the process requires more concentration, time and mental effort.

This is why reading speed should not be confused with reading ability. Someone who reads slowly may still understand the meaning, recognise important ideas and form thoughtful responses.

What Words May Look Like

Some individuals with dyslexia describe words appearing to shift, swap or blur on the page. These are a few commonly reported examples (Eide & Eide, 2026).

Letter Order Swap

"was" "saw"

The same letters may appear to be in a different order.

Mirrored Letters

"b" b ("d")

Similarly shaped letters like b/d or p/q can be confused.

Jumping / Swimming Letters

jump

Letters may seem to move, float or blur while trying to focus.

Not everyone with dyslexia experiences these effects, and dyslexia is not simply "seeing letters backwards" — the core difficulty is in connecting written letters to their sounds. These visuals are simplified illustrations, not a diagnostic tool.

4 Common Signs of Dyslexia

A person with dyslexia may (World Health Organization, 2026):

Read slowly or hesitantly
Find spelling difficult or inconsistent
Struggle to sound out unfamiliar words
Confuse visually similar words or letters
Lose their place while reading
Reread sentences several times
Find sequences difficult to remember
Need more time for reading & writing
Not every person with dyslexia will experience all these signs. Similar difficulties can also have other causes, so these signs should not be used as a diagnosis by themselves. A formal assessment should be completed by a qualified professional when appropriate.

5 Dyslexia Is More Common Than Many People Think

The British Dyslexia Association estimates that approximately 10% of the population may be dyslexic (British Dyslexia Association, 2026). This is around one person in every ten.

Visual Statistic

1 in Every 10 Individuals

That person could be someone in your classroom, workplace, family or community. However, dyslexia is not always immediately noticeable. Some people develop personal strategies to manage their difficulties, while others may remain unidentified for many years (Dyslexia Association of Singapore, 2026).

Greater awareness can help reduce harmful assumptions. Instead of labelling someone as slow, careless or unprepared, we can consider whether the information has been presented in a way that is accessible to them.

6 Dyslexia Does Not Limit Success

Dyslexia can make certain reading and writing activities more challenging, but it does not prevent someone from learning, creating, leading or succeeding.

Many people with dyslexia develop strengths in areas such as visual thinking, creativity, problem-solving, communication and reasoning (Eide & Eide, 2026). The British Dyslexia Association notes that the abilities and talents of dyslexic individuals can become more visible when they receive suitable support (British Dyslexia Association, 2026).

Entrepreneurship

Richard Branson

Founder of Virgin Group (Branson, 2026)

Has spoken publicly about how dyslexia helped him think differently, innovate, and delegate effectively.

Leadership

Lee Kuan Yew

Founding Prime Minister of Singapore (Lee, 2026)

Disclosed that he had dyslexia as an adult, showing that a reading difference does not prevent a person from becoming an influential leader.

Success should not be measured by how quickly someone reads a page. People can process information differently and still contribute valuable ideas, skills and perspectives.

7 What Can Help Dyslexic Readers?

Small adjustments can make reading materials easier to access. The purpose is not to oversimplify information, but to provide readers with different ways to receive and understand it.

Additional reading and writing time reduces pressure and allows the reader to process information carefully. This can be especially helpful during examinations, presentations or tasks involving long instructions.
Audiobooks, text-to-speech tools and recorded instructions allow readers to listen while following the written text. Audio should be offered as an alternative format rather than treated as an easier or less valid way of learning.
Readable font sizes, short paragraphs, clear headings and sufficient spacing can make content easier to follow. Important information should not be placed inside large, crowded blocks of text.
A ruler, bookmark, digital line guide or highlighted section can help readers remain focused on the correct line and reduce the likelihood of losing their place.
Diagrams, illustrations, timelines, icons and charts can reinforce the meaning of written information. Visuals should support the text rather than decorate the page without a clear purpose.

8 Inclusive Reading Resources

If you have dyslexia, these are a few resources that may genuinely make reading easier — from audiobooks to books designed specifically for dyslexic readers, to free tools that adapt any text on screen.

Audio Formats

Audiobooks & Audio Versions

Listening to a book while following the text can ease the strain of decoding every word. Learning Ally offers a large library of human-narrated audiobooks built specifically for students with dyslexia, with audio and text synced together.

Visit Learning Ally
Accessible Library

Accessible Digital Library

Bookshare is an online library built for people with print disabilities, including dyslexia. It lets you adjust font, spacing and line length, or have any book read aloud — so you can pick the format that works for you.

Visit Bookshare
Dyslexia-Friendly Books

Books Designed for Dyslexic Readers

Barrington Stoke publishes real, engaging books written and formatted specifically for dyslexic and reluctant readers — using a dyslexia-friendly font, cream paper to reduce glare, and shorter chapters.

Visit Barrington Stoke
Reading Assistant Tool

Turn Any Page Dyslexia-Friendly

HelperBird is a free browser-based reading assistant that adapts text on any website or document — dyslexia-friendly fonts, text-to-speech, colour overlays, and spacing adjustments, all in one toolbar.

Visit HelperBird

9 Accessibility Tips for Digital Content

To make blogs and learning resources more inclusive, creators can follow these practical guidelines (W3C, 2026; British Dyslexia Association, 2026):

Use a clear font at a comfortable size
Keep text aligned to the left
Use short paragraphs and meaningful headings
Leave sufficient space between lines and sections
Avoid writing long passages in ALL CAPS or italics
Maintain strong contrast between text and background
Use bullet points for steps or related ideas
Explain unfamiliar terms clearly
Add captions or transcripts to audio and video
Include alternative text for meaningful images
Allow users to zoom without losing content
Avoid distracting animations behind written text

Accessibility should not be treated as an additional feature for a small group of people. Clear structure and flexible content formats can improve the reading experience for everyone.

10 Creating a More Understanding Reading Culture

Supporting dyslexic readers begins with understanding that different does not mean less capable.

A person may read at a different speed, use a different strategy or require another format. They can still understand the same message, develop meaningful ideas and achieve important goals.

Different speed. Different process.

The same right to read, learn and understand.
